title: A Pivotal Moment
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Writing to what she calls soulful leaders, Schafer argues that leadership is not an external thing handled by someone more powerful but a capacity each person carries. She names two corrosive beliefs, that someone else will take care of things and that we ourselves are incapable of shaping our communities, and blames systems that concentrate responsibility at the top. Her move is to redefine responsibility as response-ability, the ability to respond to what life asks, grounded in trust rather than control. She calls the result citizen leadership, expressed through presence, choice and participation starting in family, workplace and neighbourhood. The piece is reflective and framed by a current civic moment, but its argument about distributed leadership is clear, and reflection questions close it.
points: Responsibility has been distorted into weight, control and dominance; the author reclaims it as the capacity to respond.
Concentrating responsibility at the top teaches everyone else to disengage and see themselves as replaceable parts.
Small acts, how we listen, care and show up, are presented as the living foundation of shared governance rather than peripheral.
Citizen leadership is defined by presence and participation instead of title, beginning where you are and spreading through relationships.
The reflection questions ask readers to spot where they confused responsibility with weight and where they stepped back waiting for someone else.
quotes: First, many of us have been lulled into the belief that someone else, someone smarter, stronger, wealthier, or more powerful, will take care of “things” for us. That leadership is something external. That responsibility belongs elsewhere.
Over time, responsibility became distorted. Instead of representing agency and dignity, it became synonymous with pressure, control, and dominance.

In our relentless focus on the “big” things, big leaders, big systems, big solutions, we lost sight of the quiet power and necessity of the small things: how we show up for one another, how we listen, how we care, how we choose to participate in the lives directly in front of us. We forgot that these small acts are not peripheral to democracy; they are its living foundation.

Responsibility, at its essence, is response-ability: the ability to respond to what life is asking of us. It arises not from force or hierarchy, but from trust, the belief that people are capable of discernment, contribution, and care.

Not leadership defined by title or control, but leadership expressed through presence, choice, and participation. Leadership that begins exactly where you are, within your family, your neighborhood, your workplace, your community, and extends outward through relationships rather than mandates.
We do not need to become more than we are. We need only to become more present to what we already carry.
